Sustainable PPE Plastics: A Historical 2030 Market Scenario

A sustainable product claim must meet the same performance and traceability test as the product itself.

Pupsi Phull · Phull Insights22 September 20262 min readSustainable Performance
Evidence boundary

Personal analysis and professional reflection based on earlier postgraduate work. Named-company examples describe historical research, not current 2026 corporate policies, figures or commitments. No unpublished case result is represented as a verified outcome.

Why this matters

Protective equipment presents a difficult materials challenge. Substitution, recycling and take-back ideas have to be tested against safety, product standards, cost and the reality of collection after use.

What the evidence suggests

The original postgraduate proposal used a 2030 market scenario and suggested ambitious supplier targets. Its market sizing, share estimates and regulatory forecasts were assumptions of that research period, not verified current facts or RS Group commitments.

What it looks like in practice

A credible programme would start by separating product categories, understanding material composition and checking what alternatives can meet required performance. Supplier collaboration and a bounded pilot come before a portfolio-wide promise.

Practical next steps

Three things leaders can do now

01

Ask suppliers for product-level material and performance evidence.

02

Pilot one feasible category with clear safety and end-of-life criteria.

03

Publish only targets with an agreed baseline, accountable owner and verification method.

Phull Insights Perspective

The view beneath the headline.

The opportunity is to make circularity measurable without compromising protection. A bold number is not a strategy until the supply chain can support it.
